title: How many runs do I need?
question: How many tasks and runs does it take to see a difference, and how small a difference can I hope to see?
what_you_learn: What power is, and how the smallest detectable difference shrinks as the number of runs grows.
Why more tasks usually help more than more runs of the same task.
How to read the detectable number on Run setup, and what it assumes.

know: What a 95% interval is, from the article on comparing runs fairly.

sections.heading: Two ways to be wrong
body: A comparison can go wrong in two ways. It can report a difference that is only noise, a false alarm. Or it can miss a difference that is real.

The 5% level limits false alarms: when nothing changed, a 95% interval misses zero by chance about 1 time in 20. Power limits misses. It is the chance of detecting a difference of a given size when that difference is real.
The usual target is 80% power at the 5% level. Miller (2024) uses this pair in his worked example for model evals. The classic guide to planning a study this way is Cohen's book on power analysis.

sections.heading: The smallest detectable difference
body: Turn the question around. With the runs you can afford, what is the smallest true difference you would detect 80% of the time? Miller calls it the minimum detectable effect; TraceHarness says smallest detectable difference.
It shrinks with the square root of the number of runs. Four times the runs only halves it.

Run setup uses the simplest version. An arm is one side of the comparison, such as the runs under one harness. For n runs in each arm, the detectable difference is 2.8 x the square root of 0.5 / n. The 2.8 is 1.96 for the 5% level plus 0.84 for 80% power. The 0.5 assumes the worst case, a pass rate near 50%.

list: To detect 10 points you need 392 runs per arm; to detect 5 points, 1,568.

sections.heading: Tasks or repeats?
body: That formula treats every run as independent. Runs of the same task are not: they share the code, the issue and the difficulty. So the formula gives a floor, not a promise.
Miller splits the noise in two parts. Each question has its own difficulty, and each answer adds noise around it. Asking the same question again shrinks only the second part.
In his example, going from 1 to 10 answers per question cut the detectable difference from 13.2% to 7.5%. Past some point, more answers per question change little; only more questions help.

Agents add the same second part. Bjarnason et al. (2026) ran agents many times on SWE-bench Verified (500 real GitHub issues that developers screened). Their pass@1, the share of tasks one run solves, moved by 2.2 to 6.0 points depending on which run was picked.
They recommend several runs per task, and a power analysis to choose how many runs you need before you start.

The figure below shows it on gemini-2.5-flash-lite's 24 tasks under baseline. With 1 run per task, a 95% interval is about plus or minus 19.4 points if runs are counted, and 19.8 if tasks are. With 5 runs per task, the first shrinks to 8.7 and the second stays at 18.9.

olist: Decide the smallest difference that would change what you do.
Read Run setup's detectable number for your plan before you launch it.
Add tasks first. Add repeats until each task's own rate stops moving much, then stop.
If the interval covers 0, say that no difference was detected at this sample size. Do not say there was none.

worked_example.title: What 24 tasks can and cannot detect

dataset.name: study_v04
dataset.what: Bundled with the study copy: 3,240 recorded runs, 3 models x 9 harnesses x 24 small Python tasks x 5 runs. They were collected through OpenRouter (a paid service that passes requests on to many model providers) at temperature 0.
dataset.credit: TraceHarness bundled data (AURA lab, William & Mary).

open: Click the dataset name at the top of the left list and choose study_v04.
Click Analysis, then Run setup, and read the plan's estimate.
Click Analysis, then Comparison, and read the gemini-2.5-flash-lite row.
body: Run setup's first plan is one model and one harness on all 24 tasks, 3 runs each: 72 runs. It reports a detectable difference of 23.3 points per arm.
The recorded cells have 5 runs per task, so 120 runs per arm. The same formula gives 18.1 points.

gemini-2.5-flash-lite passed 75 of 120 runs under baseline and 98 of 120 under reprompt. The paired difference is +19.2 points, with 6 tasks better and none worse. That is just above 18.1, and the Comparison page marks it separates.
Now look inside the tasks. Under baseline, 22 of the 24 tasks either passed all 5 runs or failed all 5. For those tasks, five repeats told the same story five times.

That is why the task, not the run, is the unit (the thing you count as one independent measurement). Treating the 120 runs as independent gives a 95% interval of about plus or minus 8.7 points around 62.5%. Using the 24 task rates gives about plus or minus 18.9 points.
So 18.1 points is a floor for this design. To detect a difference of 10 points, add tasks; more runs of these 24 would mostly repeat themselves.

clicks: Click the dataset name at the top of the left list and choose study_v04.
Read the detectable value of the first plan. Then click Change the plan, raise Runs per task from 3 to 5, and read it again.
try_it.question: What detectable difference does the plan report with 3 runs per task, and with 5? Using the formula, how many runs per arm would 10 points take?
try_it.answer: 23.3 points per arm with 3 runs per task (72 runs), and 18.1 points with 5 (120 runs). 10 points takes 392 runs per arm. With 24 tasks that is 17 runs per task, so adding tasks is the better way there.
try_it.answer_measured_from: Run setup page, Estimate: detectable per arm. The formula in traceharness/frontend/src/rig/views/analysis.jsx: 2.8 x sqrt(0.5 / n). For 10 points: n = 2.8^2 x 0.5 / 0.1^2 = 392, and 392 / 24 rounds up to 17.

quiz.q: You quadruple the number of runs per arm. What happens to the smallest detectable difference?
options: It drops to a quarter of what it was before
It does not change at all
It doubles, because there is more noise
It halves: it shrinks with the square root
quiz.why: The detectable difference shrinks with the square root of the sample: four times the runs halves it.

quiz.q: Most tasks pass all their runs or fail all of them. What should you add to detect a smaller difference?
options: More runs of the same tasks
quiz.why: When runs of a task agree, repeats add little; the noise that matters comes from which tasks you have.

quiz.q: A planned comparison covers 0. What may you say?
options: No difference was detected at this sample size
The two setups perform the same on these tasks
The harness change made no difference to the runs
The result proves that the change is harmful
quiz.why: An interval that covers 0 shows no difference was detected at this sample size. It does not show there is none; a narrow interval only rules out large differences.

in_short: **Power is the chance of detecting a real difference**; the usual target is 80% power at the 5% level.
**The smallest detectable difference shrinks with the square root of the runs**: 120 runs per arm detect about 18.1 points, and four times the runs only halve it.
Runs of one task are not independent, so **add tasks first; more repeats of the same tasks mostly repeat themselves**.
